books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: Maria W. Stewart, address at Franklin Hall, Boston, September 21, 1832

stimulus.text:
The church: In 1816, Richard Allen and other Black Methodist ministers in Philadelphia formed the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first independent Black denomination in the United States. Allen, who had bought his own freedom from slavery, became its first bishop. Black Methodists had left white-led churches after Black worshippers were pulled from their knees at prayer.

The speaker: "Tell us no more of southern slavery; for with few exceptions, although I may be very erroneous in my opinion, yet I consider our condition but little better than that." — Maria W. Stewart, speaking at Franklin Hall, Boston, September 21, 1832.

The school: In 1833, Prudence Crandall, a white Quaker teacher, opened a school for Black girls in Canterbury, Connecticut. Townspeople attacked the school and forced it to close in 1834.

The stories and songs: Enslaved people told Br’er Rabbit stories, in which the weak rabbit outwits the strong, and made music on fiddles and banjos built from gourds and horsehair, mixing African and Southern traditions.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 B, with the Stewart quotation verbatim from her September 21, 1832 address at Franklin Hall, Boston, and the Crandall facts checked against the Oxford African American Studies Center chronology.

options.text: white Northerners generally welcomed Black education and Black public speech in the 1830s
options.misconception: Townspeople attacked the school, and Stewart faced ridicule.

options.text: education and public speech were contested paths to equality in the 1830s
Black girls in Connecticut could attend any school they chose
options.misconception: Crandall’s school was attacked and closed.

options.text: the federal government ran schools for free Black children
options.misconception: No federal role is shown anywhere in the passage.

rationales.A: Welcome is the wrong word. A mob attacked Crandall’s school, and Stewart was ridiculed for speaking.
rationales.B: Stewart claimed a public voice and Crandall opened a school for Black girls. Both efforts met open attack from white neighbors.
rationales.C: Black girls could not attend any school they chose. The one school built for them was attacked until it closed.
rationales.D: The federal government runs no school in this passage. Crandall’s school was a private effort.
rationales.general:
1. Put the two cases together. A Black woman speaks in public; a white teacher opens a school for Black girls.
2. Note the response to each. Stewart faced ridicule; townspeople attacked Crandall’s school until it closed.
3. Name the pattern. Claiming education and a public voice met open resistance.
Background: Stewart gave her farewell address in 1833; Crandall’s school closed in 1834.
Remember: when two different efforts meet the same attack, the attack is the pattern.
